newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BAGGIO, DEL PIERO SUFFER CONTRASTING FORTUNES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BAGGIO, DEL PIERO SUFFER CONTRASTING FORTUNES.

text.p: Roberto Baggio was never a member of the Dead Poet's Society but Oscar Washington Tabarez would doubtless have given him a role in the Hollywood hit film.

"Sadly, there's no place for poets in modern soccer," said Milan's Uruguayan coach, who has recently relegated the former European footballer of the year and Italian international to the substitute's bench.

Baggio is better known as a Buddhist than a Romanticist, but Tabarez's epitaph no doubt had him casting a nostalgic glance toward the green, green fields of Turin's Stadio Delle Alpi where Juventus will play Milan this weekend.
There, while playing for Juventus between 1990 and 1995, Baggio's unique soccer artistry brought him 78 goals in 141 matches and the nickname of 'Raffaele' after the great Renaissance painter.
To make matters worse, Baggio's successor at Juve, Alessandro Del Piero, is already being likened to another classic Italian painter, 'Pinturicchio'.

The 22-year-old midfielder, who inherited Baggio's famous number 10 shirt in 1995 in only his second full season in serie A, offers living proof that fantasy can still triumph over physique in modern day soccer.

Del Piero is already Juve's third all-time goalscorer in the European Cup with eight goals -- behind the illustrious names of Paolo Rossi and Michel Platini -- and back on form after a 17-day lay-off with a twisted knee.
And like Baggio, Del Piero has acquired legendary status.

Three curling shots, each one a carbon copy of the other, from the far side of the penalty area into the top corner of the net in last year's European Cup, prompted Juve fans to re-christian that part of the Delle Alpi goal as " the Del Piero angle".
On Sunday, on his old home ground and against his great rival, Baggio should have the perfect chance to prove he, too, can still write his own version of soccer poetry -- if he plays.
"I even don't know if I figure in his (Tabarez's) plans," Baggio told Gazzetta dello Sport this week.
Since joining Milan in the summer of 1995, Baggio has struggled with knee injuries, and is only now starting to look and play like his old self.
But not even a vintage goal in Milan's 1-1 Italian Cup quarter-final draw with his first-ever club Vicenza on Tuesday could persuade Tabarez to make Baggio an automatic choice.
"Baggio might play on Sunday," was as much as Tabarez would concede after the match.
The Uruguayan dropped Baggio after starting the season with a 4-3-1-2 formation that sought to combine Marco Simone and George Weah with the gifted playmaker.

But Baggio's apparent unwillingness to chase back and cover forced Tabarez to accomodate him on the right-side of midfield. When that, too, failed, he was dropped in favour of youngster Tomas Locatelli.
Against Vicenza, Baggio even spent 45 minutes playing centre-half.
While Baggio remains a free spirit in a game that is becoming ever more a prisoner to tacticians, Del Piero has learned to adapt his flair to disciplinarian Juventus coach Marcello Lippi.

Last year, Del Piero even sacrificed his natural eye for goal to play a deeper defensive role in midfield. "It was tough," he recalled, "I found that by the time I got close to the goal, I lacked the lucidity to score. But that's soccer today."

It is not a situation that pleases everyone. In the wake of Juve's Italian Cup quarter-final defeat by Inter on Wednesday, sports daily Gazzetta dello Sport lambasted Lippi's decision to field Del Piero in midfield.
"Forced to be a workhorse, what a pity to see him reduced to this," commented the paper.
At least Del Piero is guaranteed a starting place against Milan.
But, even if Baggio does start on the bench, Juve should be warned -- he has scored three goals this season going on as a sub.
And, as Del Piero himself pointed out this week, for a class player, it only takes a back-heel to write yourself in the history books.
